Key findings
  • Repeat tests of the same tyre under the same conditions differ by about 0.036 in peak µ. That alone caps the R² of any model at 0.92 for single tests (0.98 for averages of repeats).
  • Slip at peak µ is mostly measurement scatter (ceiling R² 0.16); predict it as a typical value with a wide range.
  • A reference tyre is run between candidates. Its level drifts between sessions, and candidate tyres move with it (r = 0.38). The test day accounts for about 5% of the variation in peak µ. Results are therefore also given day-corrected.
  • A: tested tyre, new condition: peak µ R² 0.85, typical error 0.051 µ on held-out tyres. Without day correction: R² 0.79, error 0.062 µ; with it the error is 0.051 µ. (R² can fall while the error shrinks: the correction removes day-to-day variation, so less variation is left to explain.)
  • B: known compound, new size: peak µ R² 0.84, typical error 0.045 µ on held-out tyres. Without day correction: R² 0.79, error 0.054 µ; with it the error is 0.045 µ. (R² can fall while the error shrinks: the correction removes day-to-day variation, so less variation is left to explain.)
  • C: new compound: peak µ R² 0.80, typical error 0.057 µ on held-out tyres. Without day correction: R² 0.76, error 0.063 µ; with it the error is 0.057 µ. (R² can fall while the error shrinks: the correction removes day-to-day variation, so less variation is left to explain.)

1. The data

The master has 542 distinct IDs; 542 curve files were found and 541 matched an ID (rule: the number at the start of the file name). 1 master rows have no file, 1 files have no master row, 0 IDs have more than one file.

2. Data quality and recommendations

Every master row and curve file was checked. Errors make a value unusable (it is excluded or replaced); warnings are usable but worth a look; info items were corrected automatically. The full list is in data_quality_flags.csv.

3. Statistical analysis

4. Pacejka (Magic Formula) fitting

Each curve was fitted with µ = D·sin(C·atan(B·s − E·(B·s − atan(B·s)))) on slip 0-0.90, once with B, C, D, E free and once with C fixed per surface (median of the free fits: Dry 1.59, Wet 1.85). D equals peak µ, B·C·D the initial slope.

5. Train-test split and unbalanced sizes

How the data is split decides what the score means. A random split puts repeat tests of the same tyre in both training and test, so the model only has to recognise a tyre it has already seen. Each case below hides exactly what would be unknown in practice:

  • A, tested tyre at a new condition: whole configurations are hidden; scored only where the same tyre was tested at other conditions.
  • B, known compound in a new size: one size at a time is hidden; scored on compounds also tested in another size.
  • C, new compound: whole compound groups are hidden, in every size.

Does the model learn more from the majority sizes?

7. Predicting an untested tyre

The saved predictor (predictor.joblib) decides the case for each new tyre (A if the same size+pattern+compound was tested, B if the compound was tested in another size, C otherwise), uses the best model for that case, and returns the landmarks with 90% ranges, B, C, D, E and the full curve, built from the landmarks so that all of them agree exactly. Predictions are for an average test day (day-corrected).

8. Recommendations

  • Fix the 4 data errors at the source (see section 2a): duplicate IDs, out-of-range master values, unreadable files. Each fix returns a test to the analysis.
  • Repeat scatter is the hard limit. Peak µ repeats differ by 0.036. The average of n repeats is uncertain by 0.036/√n: 0.021 for 3, 0.015 for 6. Report and model averages of repeats, and judge models against the ceiling, not against 1.0.
  • Use the reference tyre to correct for the test day. Candidates move with the reference (r = 0.38). Keep running it at least once per session, ideally before and after each candidate block.
  • Slip at peak µ is dominated by scatter. The rig records only a few points between 3% and 30% slip, so the peak location is coarse. Denser sampling or a slower sweep around the peak would make it predictable; until then use typical values per surface with the reported range.
  • Break the compound-size link. Testing a few existing compounds in additional sizes is the cheapest way to make case B (and C) predictable. Suggested first tests below.
  • Always measure DMA and footprint for a new tyre before predicting: they carry the compound information, and the predictor's accuracy for new compounds depends on them.
  • Quote accuracy per case (A/B/C) and never from a random split of tests.

9. Method notes

  • Curve files are matched to master rows by the number at the start of the file name; slip in percent and negative sign conventions are corrected automatically; isolated spikes are removed.
  • Landmarks are read from each curve the same way for every test: peak µ and its slip from the lightly smoothed curve, µ slide at 90% slip, µ lock as the mean µ above 95% slip, initial slope below 3% slip. Master values are used where no usable curve exists.
  • Magic Formula fits use slip 0-0.90 (the lock-up drop beyond is not Magic-Formula shaped). Predicted curves are Magic Formula up to 0.90, then a straight blend to the predicted µ lock.
  • All scores are on tyres hidden from training. 90% ranges are cross-conformal: the range for each fold is set from the errors on the other folds, and its coverage is checked.
  • Every model was run with three imbalance options (as is, sizes re-weighted 1/√n, repeats averaged per configuration); the best per case and landmark is kept. Picking the best of many set-ups flatters it slightly: treat differences below ~0.02 in R² as noise.
